verse:
praśāmyadbhāvayeccakraṃ tataḥ śāntaṃ tataḥ śamam /
anena dhy

evaṃ pratikṣaṇaṃ viśvaṃ svasaṃvidi vilāpayan /
visṛjaṃśca ta

translation: Thus, beginning from the triśūla (the trident), in the successive order of the four-spoked and five-spoked (wheels), up to the fifty-spoked (wheel), the yogin should bring the wheel (cakra) into being (contemplate it).

terms.tri\u015b\u016bla: trident — the three-pronged form that is the point of departure of the series; here syntactically the starting point (triśūlāt prabhṛti), not itself called a cakra
terms.catu\u1e63pa\u00f1c\u0101raka: the four- and five-spoked (wheels) — dvandva compound (catuḥ + pañcāraka) naming the intermediate wheels of the sequence
terms.pa\u00f1c\u0101\u015badara: fifty-spoked — the terminal wheel (pañcāśat 'fifty' + ara 'spoke'); traditionally the wheel whose spokes are the fifty varṇas (mātṛkā phonemes)
terms.cakra: wheel — the visualized circular diagram of spokes within the body, each spoke bearing a tattva/varṇa
terms.krama: succession, due order — the ordered progression of the wheels
terms.vibh\u0101vayet: should cause to arise / should visualize — causative optative of vi-√bhū; the yogin actively brings the wheel to presence in meditation

contested: 1) Parsing of catuṣpañcārakakramāt: standard reading is a dvandva, 'in the order of the four- and five-spoked (wheels)'; alternatively 'four five-spoked (wheels)' (catuṣ = four, pañcāraka = five-spoked), which would change the sequence. 2) Whether the series is a complete numerical progression (3, 4, 5 … 50 spokes, i.e. dozens of intermediate wheels) or a select enumerated set — the verse names only the 4- and 5-spoked steps before leaping to the fifty-spoked end, so the intermediate counts are implicit and contested. 3) The referent of pañcāśadara: the fifty phonemes of the mātṛkā is the traditional identification, but the verse itself does not state it; readings as fifty tattva-classes or śakti-counts also circulate. 4) Whether triśūla is itself the first (three-spoked) cakra or a distinct prior form: the syntax triśūlāt prabhṛti … cakraṃ vibhāvayet presents the trident as the starting point of the meditation, with the object of vibhāvayet being the wheel, so the trident's status within the cakra-series remains open.

translation: Of the Lord of consciousness — the great God whose consciousness shines forth — there is no kalanā (limitation) whatsoever; nor of the universal Power, nor of the Great Lord.

terms.sa\u1e43vinn\u0101tha: Lord of consciousness — saṃvid ('awareness, consciousness') + nātha ('lord'); the supreme subject, consciousness itself as sovereign
terms.ull\u0101sisa\u1e43vida\u1e25: gen. sg. of the bahuvrīhi ullāsisaṃvid, 'he whose consciousness is radiant'; ullāsa = shining forth / bursting forth / expansion
terms.kalan\u0101: limitation, particularization — from √kal 'to count, reckon, delimit'; the delimiting operation that cuts the one into finite determinations
terms.vi\u015bva\u015bakti: universal power — the all-pervading śakti of the Lord, the dynamic face of consciousness
terms.mahe\u015bit\u1e5b: the Great Lord (mahā + īśitṛ 'ruler') — epithet of Śiva as sovereign

contested: kalanā is the crux: cognate with vikalpa, it names the limiting/particularizing activity by which the unlimited is apprehended as many; renderings range from 'limitation' and 'restriction' to 'imposition' and 'imaginative construction.' The verse denies it absolutely of the ultimate reality. Syntax is also contested: the genitives may be read either as one reality in apposition (the Lord of consciousness = the great radiant God = possessor of the universal power = Maheśitṛ — the Kashmir Śaiva reading) or as a graded series (consciousness, its power, and the Lord as substrate). Minor fork: ullāsisaṃvidaḥ could be parsed as tatpuruṣa ('radiance of consciousness') rather than bahuvrīhi; and the register of viśvaśakti is close to Krama usage of the universal power of consciousness.

translation: One whose mind is fixed on nothing else should meditate upon the wheel — whether it has sixty-four spokes, or a thousand spokes, or countless thousands of spokes.

terms.cakra: wheel / disc of light — the meditative wheel of consciousness-radiance; not a corporeal chakra
terms.catu\u1e63\u1e63a\u1e63\u1e6di\u015bat\u: having sixty-four spokes (catuṣṣaṣṭi + śatāra 'spoked'); the 64 evoke the kalās / energies
terms.asa\u1e43khy\u0101rasahasram: having countless thousands of spokes (asaṃkhyāra 'uncountable-spoked' + sahasram) — the final, unbounded member of the gradation
terms.ar\u0101 / \u015bat\u0101ra: spokes; also 'rays' — ara means both a wheel's spoke and a ray of light, and here the two converge
terms.dhy\u0101yet: should meditate (3rd sg. optative of √dhyai) — prescriptive injunction
terms.ananyadh\u012b\u1e25: whose intellect is directed to no other [object] — single-pointed (ekāgra)

contested: 1) ara: 'spoke' vs 'ray' — in the tantric cakra both readings converge: the spokes are the rays of prakāśa, and the wheel is best taken as the raśmicakra of universal light. 2) asaṃkhyārasahasram: 'countless thousands (of spokes)' vs 'a thousand of uncountable spokes' — the number is indeterminate either way; the point is the graded ascent 64 → 1000 → uncountable from determinate form toward the infinite, so the verse gives one object at increasing scope, not three alternatives. 3) catuṣṣaṣṭiśatāram: the long ā settles 'having 64 spokes'; a numeral reading '164' (catuḥṣaṣṭiśata) would require short a. 4) The cakra is not a haṭhayogic bodily cakra — in TA 5 it is the wheel of light of consciousness, and 'ananyadhīḥ' marks the meditation as ekāgra, free of any second object.

translation: By this very way one should also resort to the other meditations, which attain the foremost rank (dhurā) of the Anuttara upāya without sequence.

terms.anuttarop\u0101ya: the unsurpassed means — the highest of the Trika upāyas, the means whose ground is Anuttara (supreme consciousness, Paramaśiva); retained as a technical term, not rendered
terms.dhur\u0101: lit. 'yoke-pole / burden' of a wagon; idiomatically 'the foremost station, the leading office' — the meditations come to occupy the very eminence of the highest means
terms.di\u015b\u0101: 'way, path' — the meditative course laid out in the immediately preceding verses, back-referenced by anayā ... eva ('this very')
terms.krama: 'sequence, graded order' — the graduated progression of the lower upāyas (āṇava → śākta → śāmbhava)
terms.sam\u0101\u015brayet: 'one should resort to / take recourse to / adopt' — optative, prescriptive
terms.\u0101y\u0101nti: 'they come, they attain' (ā-√i); construed with dhurāṃ: 'come to the burden of'

contested: dhurā is the crux: literal 'yoke-pole/burden' vs. the idiom 'foremost place' — i.e. whether the other meditations come to BEAR the office of the Anuttara upāya (function as it) or merely approach its level; the verb ā-√i with dhurāṃ idiomatically favors 'attain the eminence of'. anuttara is a loaded technical term (the supreme reality; also identified with the śāmbhava upāya), so anuttaropāya may be read 'the highest means' or 'the means that is Anuttara itself'. kramaṃ vinā is contested as to what sequence is bypassed: the graded order of upāyas, or sequence as such (the timeless immediacy characteristic of the highest means). diśā is sometimes loosened to 'in this manner' rather than a specific prior path.

verse:
śaktayo@sya jagat kṛtsnaṃ śaktimāṃstu maheśvaraḥ /
iti māṅga
translation: His śaktis (powers) are this entire world (jagat); the śaktimān (Possessor of Power), however, is Maheśvara (the Great Lord). — "Thus," in the māṅgalaśāstra (the scripture of the auspicious opening), however, the venerable Śrīśrīkaṇṭha established [this teaching].

terms.\u015baktaya\u1e25 (\u015bakti): powers — the Lord's dynamic energies; the world is here declared to BE these powers (identity, not mere instrumentality)
terms.asya: his — of the Lord (sc. Maheśvara), resumed by śaktimān
terms.jagat: the world / the moving universe (lit. 'what moves', √gam); with kṛtsnam = 'the entire world'
terms.\u015baktim\u0101n: the Possessor of Power — the Lord as substrate and owner of the śaktis; the technical Śaiva counterpart of śakti (power vs. power-holder)
terms.iti: closing quotative ('thus'), marking the end of the cited statement
terms.m\u0101\u1e45gala\u015b\u0101stre: in the auspicious scripture — either the title of a specific (possibly lost) text, or descriptive: the scripture whose maṅgala (opening benediction) this very statement is
terms.\u015br\u012b\u015br\u012bka\u1e47\u1e6d: the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha — the doubled śrī is honorific; an ācārya of the Trika/Kaula transmission; the name is also an epithet of Śiva ('beautiful-throated')
terms.nyar\u016bpayat: established / set forth — 3sg imperfect of ni-√rūp 'to determine, demonstrate, teach' (rūpayati + ni, ny-arūpayat)

contested: 1) ŚRĪŚRĪKAṆṬHA: most plausibly a human ācārya of the Trika/Kaula paramparā — the name recurs in the guru-lineage of Tantrāloka 37 — but the identity is not settled; he is sometimes conflated with the Śaiva-Vedāntin Śrīkaṇṭha, author of the Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras (10th-c. Kashmir), whose corpus is Vedānta, not a māṅgalaśāstra. Since the verse says he 'established' a doctrine 'in a śāstra,' the epithet-of-Śiva reading is less likely but cannot be excluded (the doubled śrī marks reverence either way). 2) MĀṄGALAŚĀSTRA: ambiguous between a text-title and a descriptive phrase, 'the scripture [that opens] with the auspicious [statement]' — i.e. the maṅgala-section of the source tantra; no text securely titled Māṅgalaśāstra is attested, so the descriptive reading seems safer. 3) THE SECOND 'tu' (māṅgalaśāstre tu): adversative — the citation is marshalled against a rival view of the world's relation to the Lord canvassed in the surrounding verses of TA 5. 4) DOCTRINAL CRUX: does 'jagat = śakti' assert identity or efficient causality? The nominal predication without copula favors the monistic Trika reading — the world is not produced by but IS the Lord's power — continuous with Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8 (parāsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate) and the pañcaśakti doctrine; whether śakti/śaktimān here implies a real distinction (power vs. power-holder as cause vs. effect, a Sāṃkhya-flavored frame) or a purely pedagogical one within non-duality remains an open interpretive question. [X-DOCT] [X-IDEN]

verse:
atha prāṇasya yā vṛttiḥ prāṇanādyā nirūpitā /
tadupāyatayā b
translation: Now, the operation of prāṇa, beginning with respiration (prāṇanā), has been described. Since that [operation] is the means [to the supreme state], we declare the unfolding of the Higher (uttara-pravikāsana).

terms.pr\u0101\u1e47a: the vital breath / life-force; the inner breath regarded as the vehicle and locus of consciousness
terms.pr\u0101\u1e47an\u0101: respiration, the act of breathing in; first member of prāṇa's series of operations
terms.nir\u016bpit\u0101: described, set forth, investigated (pp. of nir-√ūp)
terms.tadup\u0101yatay\u0101: as the means to that / that [operation] being the means (tad-upāya-tā, f. instr.): the instrumental marks the prāṇa-operation as the upāya whose result is the higher unfolding
terms.uttara-pravik\u0101sana: the unfolding (pra-vi-√kas, lyuṭ) of the Higher: the blossoming-forth of the supreme reality/consciousness that lies beyond prāṇa; alternatively 'the further (subsequent) unfolding' of the exposition

contested: (1) tadupāyatayā: the antecedent of tad is ambiguous — either prāṇa's vṛtti ('that [vṛtti] being the means, we declare the higher unfolding', i.e. breath-operation = upāya, higher manifestation = fruit) or an implied goal ('as the means to that end'); (2) uttara-pravikāsana: whether uttara denotes the ontologically higher reality (supreme consciousness beyond prāṇa, whose self-blossoming is pravikāsana) or merely 'further' (continuation of the teaching); (3) prāṇanādyā: whether the series is just the breath-functions (prāṇanā, apāna, ...) or the full kalā-series of prāṇa, which changes how the 'means' is understood; (4) atha: a bare new-topic marker, or carrying a practice-context ('now, in this discipline') sense.

verse:
viśvaṃ bibharti pūraṇadhāraṇayogena tena ca śriyate /
savima
translation: By the union of pūraṇa (filling) and dhāraṇa (upholding) He bears the universe, and through that very deed He is glorified; being possessed of vimarśa (reflexive awareness) and having the form of rava (the primal resonant utterance), He likewise works the good of those who fear saṃsāra.

terms.p\u016bra\u1e47a: filling, permeating — the act whereby the ground of reality pours itself through the whole of the universe (cognate with sṛṣṭi, emanation)
terms.dh\u0101ra\u1e47a: upholding, sustaining — the maintenance of the world in being (cognate with sthiti, preservation)
terms.yoga: conjunction, union — the pairing of the two functions, not the Yoga school
terms.vimar\u015ba: reflexive awareness, self-consciousness — the dynamic self-referential 'I'-awareness that accompanies, and imparts reality to, the mere luminosity (prakāśa) of consciousness; the Pratyabhijñā/Tantrāloka technical term, not 'reflection'
terms.\u015briyate: is glorified, is resplendent — passive of √śrī/√śri; the Lord's glory (śrī) consists in this world-sustaining act
terms.rava: resonant sound, primal utterance — the audible/sonant unfolding of the supreme Word (parā vāc) through which the universe becomes manifest
terms.sa\u1e43s\u0101rabh\u012bru: one who fears transmigratory existence, one afraid of the cycle of birth and death
terms.hitak\u1e5bt: doer of good, benefactor — one who brings about what is beneficial

contested: 1) rava: as transmitted ('rava rūpataś ca') the word-break permits a vocative — an interlocutor named Rava — yielding 'O Rava ... and in form as well'; but the sequence savimarśatayā ... rūpataś ca (two coordinated instrumental adverbials) favors rava as the first member of a compound rava-rūpataḥ, 'the form of resonant sound,' i.e. the supreme consciousness manifesting as the primal sonant Word in the mantra/uccāra context of Āhnika 1. I adopt the compound reading as primary; the vocative cannot be excluded. 2) śriyate: 'is glorified/resplendent' (chosen) vs. 'is served/resorted to' (passive of √śri, śrayate): the universe serving the Lord. 3) tena: most naturally 'by that [act of bearing the universe]'; alternatively 'by it [the universe].' 4) pūraṇa/dhāraṇa: taken here as the cosmic emanative/sustaining functions (sṛṣṭi/sthiti); in a yogic register they could denote the breath-phases pūraka and dhāraṇa, but the universal object viśvam favors the cosmic sense. 5) The subject is unexpressed throughout (bibharti / śriyate / hitakṛt); the implied agent is the Lord / supreme consciousness, which could equally be conceived as Parā-vāc (hence He/She/It). 6) The kārikā number follows AbhT 1.96; verse segmentation and numbering vary across editions (the Muktabodha count includes commentary prose and numbers this passage differently), and the lineation given does not scan as a standard pāda division, so the canonical wording should be checked against the KSTS text.

verse:
prāṇodaye prameye tu parānandaṃ vibhāvayet /
tatrānantaprame
translation: At the rising of the prāṇa, however, he should contemplate supreme bliss (parānanda) in the object of cognition (prameya); there, at rest (nirvṛta) through the inbreath (āpāna) that fills (pūraṇa) the portions (aṃśa) of the endless object of cognition (anantaprameya).

terms.pr\u0101\u1e47odaya: the rising/emergence of the vital breath — the moment the breath stirs to move (here the onset of the respiratory cycle, the occasion for meditation)
terms.prameya: object of cognition — the third member of the Trika triad pramātṛ/pramāṇa/prameya; the reality to be known/measured, contemplated as the meditational object
terms.par\u0101nanda: supreme bliss — the bliss of the highest reality (para/ānanda), the content realized in the prameya
terms.vibh\u0101vayet: should contemplate / should cause to shine forth (optative, causative of vi-√bhū) — the yogin makes bliss appear in the object, or realizes it there
terms.p\u016bra\u1e47\u0101p\u0101na: the filling inbreath — pūraṇa (filling; the stage prāṇāyāma calls pūraka, inhalation) + āpāna (drawing-in, inhalation; distinct from apāna, the downward vital air)
terms.nirv\u1e5bta\u1e25: at rest, fulfilled, blissful — the settled state of the meditator (or, alternatively, of the breath) after the filling inbreath

contested: 1) prameye: substantive 'object of cognition' (standard, Trika triad term) vs. qualifier agreeing with prāṇodaye ('in the breath-rise that is to be known') — grammar allows both. 2) pūraṇāpāna: whether it denotes the prāṇāyāma stage pūraka (inhalation proper, in which case this verse programmatically introduces the pūraka/kumbhaka/recaka sequence) or a looser 'filling and inbreathing'; āpāna is also orthographically one vowel from apāna, and a scribal ā/a confusion would change the physiology completely. 3) nirvṛtaḥ: bahuvrīhi on the implied yogin ('he is at rest') vs. agreement with an implied prāṇaḥ ('the breath having come to rest' — i.e., retention after the fill). 4) vibhāvayet: full causative force ('cause bliss to manifest') vs. simple 'meditate upon' — the causative is frequent in Abhinava but often weakened.

verse:
nijānande pramātraṃśamātre hṛdi purā sthitaḥ /
śūnyatāmātrav

translation: Established in supreme bliss (parānanda), let him abide, resplendent with the moon of the apāna (the downward breath); then, through the exclusive contact with the knowables (meya) flashing forth without end, he is utterly at rest.

terms.par\u0101nanda: supreme bliss — the highest of the graded bliss-stages (ānanda → prakaśānanda → vimarśānanda → parānanda) in the āveśa sequence; retained as a technical term
terms.ti\u1e63\u1e6dhet: let him abide / remain (optative of √sthā — an injunction to stay in that state)
terms.ap\u0101na: the downward vital air, prāṇa's lower counterpart, regulated in the breath-practice
terms.\u015ba\u015bi: moon — the cooling, luminous (candra/idā) aspect that ornaments the state; lit. 'adorned with the moon of apāna'
terms.meya: knowable — the object of cognition, the world as it appears to awareness
terms.sa\u1e43gha\u1e6d\u1e6da: contact / union — the coming-together of awareness with its flashing object
terms.nirv\u1e5bta\u1e25: at rest, pacified, released (pp. of nir√vṛ)

contested: apānaśaśi: the compound forks between karmadhāraya ('apāna, which is the moon' — the breath itself moon-like, cool and downward-flowing) and ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa ('the moon of/at apāna' — a moon-digit or candra-nāḍī located in apāna's region); the haṭha-style reading (lunar nectar at the lower seat) and the symbolic reading (apāna's calm luminosity) diverge here. meya: 'the knowable' may mean the external object-world or the objective content within meditation; and ananta ('endless') may be adjectival to sphuranmeya ('knowables flashing without end') or an independent substantive, yielding 'contact with knowables flashing as the Infinite'. saṃghaṭṭa: 'contact' of consciousness with objects vs. the 'collision' of prāṇa and apāna in breath-work (plausible given apāna in the first half) vs. the mutual union of subject and object in the śāktopāya manner. ekānta: whether it modifies saṃghaṭṭa ('sole/exclusive contact'), nirvṛta ('wholly at rest'), or means 'in solitude'. tataḥ: causal ('thereby') vs. merely sequential ('then'). parānanda: fixed fourth ānanda-stage vs. generic 'supreme bliss' — its status as a rung of the ānanda-ladder is itself contested in the secondary literature.

translation: Having come to the level of equality (samānabhūmi), he becomes one whose whole being is the bliss of Brahman (brahmānandamaya). And even from that (state), he is intent upon devouring (grāsa) the reckoning (kalanā) of the entire flood (augha) of means of knowing (māna) and knowables (meya).

terms.sam\u0101nabh\u016bmi: the 'level of equality' — the ground of samatā reached when prāṇa and apāna (or, more broadly, the subject–object poles) are equalized; the precondition for the arising of brahmānanda
terms.brahm\u0101nandamaya: 'made of the bliss of Brahman' — the second grade in the graded bliss-ascent (after nijānanda); the yogi's whole bodymind is pervaded by it
terms.m\u0101na: means of knowing (pramāṇa) — the cognizing pole
terms.kalan\u0101: reckoning / mental elaboration — the cognitive activity that constructs the māna–meya duality
terms.augha: 'flood' — the boundless stream/mass of such cognitions
terms.gr\u0101sa: 'devouring' — the absorption of objectivity into consciousness; the yogi swallows the entire epistemic universe

contested: samānabhūmi: (a) the state where prāṇa and apāna are equalized (samāna as the vital air / prāṇāpāna-samīkaraṇa) — most likely, given the prāṇāyāma context of TA 5; (b) the 'common ground' where knower and known coincide; (c) an allusion to samānanda (the fourth bliss), which would invert the canonical order (brahmānanda precedes samānanda) and is therefore less likely. tato'pi: 'even from that (brahmānanda state)' — the yogi transcends even this bliss — vs. 'moreover, beyond that'. grāsa: whether the yogi actively devours (volitional absorption) or objectivity spontaneously dissolves; a technical Trika term. kalanā: 'reckoning/counting' (the limiting construction of duality) vs. 'activity' in general. mānameyaugha: whether the flood is of actual cognitions or of their mere potentiality.

translation: Thus the venerable Lord Śambhunātha, pleased with me, set forth this meditation having the form of the first upāya; to him (as preceptor stood) the venerable Lord Sumati.

terms.prathamop\u0101ya: the first upāya — 'means' of attaining Śiva-consciousness; in the Tantrāloka's threefold scheme enumerated from the lowest (āṇava, śākta, śāmbhava), the first is the āṇavopāya, the effort-bound means of the limited individual, whose central discipline is meditation on breath and body; Tantrāloka ch. 5 expounds exactly that dhyāna
terms.dhy\u0101na: meditation — sustained contemplative focus; retained as a technical term, it is the practice that constitutes the āṇavopāya here
terms.nyar\u016bpayat: aorist 3sg. of nir-√rūp (causative): 'set forth, gave form to, expounded' — an act of teaching, not of meditating; the vi-√rūp reading ('transformed') is unsupported by the attested form
terms.\u015br\u012b\u015bambhun\u0101tha: the venerable Lord Śambhunātha — Abhinavagupta's principal teacher in the Trika/Kaula tradition and the source of this teaching
terms.me tu\u1e63\u1e6da\u1e25: 'pleased with me' — √tuṣ construed with the genitive (as in tuṣṭo'smi te); 'me' is not the object of nyarūpayat
terms.tasmai: 'to him' — dative governed by an elided predicate in the second half (see contested)
terms.\u015br\u012bsumatiprabhu: the venerable Lord Sumati — a guru in the transmission; on the primary reading, the preceptor of Śambhunātha, making the line a lineage notice

contested: 1) tasmai śrīsumatiprabhuḥ lacks a finite verb: (a) reading adopted above — elided 'guruḥ', 'to him [Śambhunātha] the venerable Lord Sumati was preceptor', recording the transmission Sumatinātha → Śambhunātha → Abhinavagupta; (b) alternative — a second doxological salutation with elided 'namaḥ' ('to him [homage]; the venerable Lord Sumati [also honored]'), which makes Sumati Abhinavagupta's own co-teacher rather than Śambhunātha's guru; the nominative prabhuḥ rules out 'homage to Sumati' directly, so (a) is grammatically cleaner. 2) prathamopāya — 'first upāya' is identified with the āṇavopāya from the standard enumeration and from ch. 5's subject-matter; a reading that takes prathama as a bare ordinal is possible but weaker. 3) nyarūpayat — the aorist's sandhi (ni + arūpayat → nyarūpayat) is occasionally misread; the sense is 'expounded', not 'he meditated'. 4) me tuṣṭaḥ — genitive with √tuṣ ('pleased with me'), not 'I, pleased'.

translation: The Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti), being free of every limiting adjunct, is quit of the adjunct called vyāna. Then indeed there arises consciousness-bliss (cidānanda), which is not augmented by the inert.

terms.mah\u0101vy\u0101pti: the Great Pervasion — the highest state of the yogic ascent (beyond jāgrat/svapna/suṣupti/turīya and beyond the vyāpti state itself), where consciousness is no longer conditioned by any bodily or vital function
terms.vy\u0101na: the fifth prāṇa, the diffusive vital air that pervades the whole body; here it stands as the last limiting adjunct (upādhi) of embodiment — the final vestige of physiological conditioning to be shed
terms.up\u0101dhi: limiting adjunct / conditioning factor — the technical term for whatever delimits or qualifies a state; renderings vary between 'adjunct', 'limitation', 'qualification', 'condition'
terms.nirup\u0101dhi: without any adjunct — the state in which no conditioning factor remains; qualifies mahāvyāpti as its defining character
terms.cid\u0101nanda: consciousness-bliss — the unitary reality of cit and ānanda (prakāśa-vimarśa); bliss is not an attribute of consciousness but its very nature
terms.ja\u1e0d\u0101nupab\u1e5b\u1e43hita: not augmented by the inert — from anu-pra-√bṛh 'to strengthen/fill out' with the negative prefix; the bliss of consciousness arises without being fed, filled out, or supported by jaḍa (matter, the body, the vital functions)

contested: 1) Whether vyāpti and mahāvyāpti are states of consciousness (avasthā) or stages of a means (upāya) — the TA 5 ascent is read both ways; 2) whether nirupādhi is a predicate ('it is without adjunct') or an appositive epithet of mahāvyāpti; 3) the force of anupabṛṃhita: 'not augmented' (not increased/enriched by the inert) vs. 'not filled out' (not constituted or supported by it) — the first favours a negative theology of self-sufficient bliss, the second a stronger ontological claim that the inert contributes nothing to it; 4) vyāna as literal breath vs. symbolic name for the last vestige of embodied conditioning — the verse's own wordplay (vyāna is the prāṇa whose pervasive function mirrors vyāpti) supports the symbolic reading.

verse:
udānavahnau viśrānto mahānandaṃ vibhāvayat /
tatra viśrāntim
translation: Having come to rest in the fire of the udāna breath and realizing the great bliss, and having attained repose there, he becomes calm in this great flame.

terms.ud\u0101na: the upward-moving vital breath, one of the five prāṇas; here experienced as fire
terms.vahni: fire — the udāna as ascending heat/energy
terms.vi\u015br\u0101nta\u1e25 / vi\u015br\u01: repose, resting — Abhinavagupta's key term for the settling of breath/awareness into a higher ground
terms.mah\u0101nanda: the great bliss realized at this stage of breath-dissolution
terms.vibh\u0101vayat: realizing / making manifest (causative of vi-√bhū), i.e. bringing the bliss to full appearance
terms.mah\u0101rci\u1e63i: in the great flame (loc. of mahā-arciṣ)

contested: 1) vibhāvayat: as printed it is the -at participle stem; editions also read vibhāvayan (regular nom. sg. of the -ant participle) — sense unaffected (realizing/manifesting). 2) udānavahni vs udānāgni: vahni/agni variants, synonyms. 3) mahārciṣi: identification contested — the flame of the central channel (suṣumnā) where the breaths dissolve, the fiery energy at the brahmarandhra, or the supreme light of consciousness (prakāśa) itself; the chapter's prāṇa-absorption frame favors the flame in which the vāyus are consumed. 4) tatra: whether it refers back to the udāna fire or to the great bliss just realized — grammar permits both; the sequence (rest in udāna → bliss → repose → pacification) suggests repose in the bliss, culminating in the great flame. 5) mahānanda: whether it is the bliss of the udāna station or the supreme bliss (paramānanda) prefigured; the verse marks the udāna as an intermediate station, not the final ground. 6) Subject is implicit: the yogin (masculine participles).

verse:
nahyatra saṃsthitiḥ kāpi vibhaktā jaḍarūpiṇaḥ /
yatra ko@pi
translation: For here — [in that state] in which there is no distinction whatsoever — there is no divided abiding of the insentient-formed at all; [it is that reality] which shines forth from every side.

terms.sa\u1e43sthiti\u1e25: abiding, settled state, existence (of the insentient as a separate entity)
terms.ja\u1e0dar\u016bpi\u1e47a\u1e25: of that whose form is insentient (gen. sg., collective for the insentient)
terms.sphurat: shines forth, flashes, pulses (√sphur, 3 sg. pres.)
terms.vi\u015bvata\u1e25: from every side, on all sides, everywhere
terms.yad: neuter relative, antecedent unexpressed — the supreme reality

contested: 1) vyavacchedaḥ — neutral 'distinction' vs. negative 'exclusion/limitation' (anyonyābhāva-style mutual delimitation, the standard KŚ sense); the verse's point is that in pure awareness no delimiting negation operates. 2) sphurat — 'shines' carries the prakāśa light-metaphor but flattens the dynamic sense of sphurattā, the vibrant self-pulsing of consciousness (vimarśa); 'pulses/flashes' is closer to the school's technical register. 3) The antecedent of yad is unexpressed: the supreme reality / consciousness itself (neut. tat/brahma) — not prakāśa (masc.). 4) jaḍarūpiṇaḥ — singular collective ('the insentient') vs. body-specific reference. 5) vibhaktā — attributive with saṃsthitiḥ ('a divided abiding') vs. predicative ('abiding as divided'); the denial is that the insentient has any separate, divided standing here. 6) atra — 'here' = in this state of the Lord/consciousness; also possibly 'in this matter/teaching'.

translation: That [state] whose awareness is unstruck (anāhata), filled with the supreme nectar — in it, bhāvanā and the rest have no principal connection at all.

terms.an\u0101hata: unstruck, i.e. not produced/conditioned by any 'striking' — no effort, object-contact, or practice generates it; spontaneous, self-established awareness
terms.param\u0101m\u1e5bta: supreme nectar — the bliss-essence of the supreme consciousness (parā saṃvit), not literal ambrosia; the internal ānanda-flow that saturates the state
terms.b\u1e5b\u1e43hita: filled with / swollen with (√bṛh, ppp; instrumental value) — the state is saturated, expanded by the nectar
terms.bh\u0101van\u0101: contemplative meditation, the characteristic practice of śāktopāya; 'ādīnām' extends it to all the other means (dhāraṇā, dhyāna, mantra, etc.)
terms.sa\u1e43gati: connection, relation — here denied of the practices relative to this state; the qualifier mukhyā leaves room for a merely secondary (gauṇa) role

contested: (1) anāhata: philosophical reading = unconditioned, spontaneous awareness (supported by the context: no primary connection of bhāvanā); the haṭha-yoga import of anāhata-cakra / anāhata-nāda ('unstruck sound') is a different tradition and should not be read in. (2) 'na mukhyā kāpi saṃgatiḥ': kāpi could intensify the negation to 'no connection whatsoever', but the presence of mukhyā favours 'no principal connection' — i.e. practices retain at most a secondary status, which is precisely Abhinavagupta's point that the highest state is not produced by means. (3) bṛṃhita as 'filled with' vs. 'strengthened by' the nectar (instrumental either way; sense barely shifts). (4) The antecedent of yat/yatra is an implied state (avasthā) of consciousness, not a person or a place — the translation must supply 'that [state]'.

translation: That very world-bliss — Śambhu has spoken (it) to us. Therein, repose (viśrānti) is to be established by means of the practice of the heart-utterance (hṛdayoccāra).

terms.jagad\u0101nanda: world-bliss: the universe as the very bliss (ānanda) of Śiva's self-awareness; in non-dual Trika the world is nothing other than the Lord's bliss (karmadhāraya: 'the bliss that is the world').
terms.vi\u015br\u0101nti: repose, coming-to-rest: the culminating state in which the world and consciousness come to rest in their own essence (Śiva); a technical term for the final term of the meditative ascent — not mere cessation but consummate absorption.
terms.h\u1e5bdayocc\u0101ra: heart-utterance: uccāra = the rising utterance/ascent of the inner breath-energy (also the mental utterance of mantras); hṛdaya = the heart, the supreme reality taken as the seat of this uccāra.
terms.yogata\u1e25: by means of yoga/practice (instrumental of yoga).
terms.\u0101dhey\u0101: to be placed / established / instilled (gerundive of ā-√dhā, 'is to be established').
terms.\u016bciv\u0101n: having spoken / (he) spoke — perfect participle (pf. of √vac).

contested: 1) hṛdayoccāra: two readings — (a) the uccāra whose seat is the heart, i.e. the meditative raising of energy/consciousness fixed at the supreme Heart (preferred: the verse prescribes a practice for realizing jagadānanda); (b) 'the utterance of the heart-mantra' (hṛdaya as mantra-name), attested in mantra-usage. The grammar allows both; context favours (a). 2) ūcivān: perfect participle with finite force ('he spoke to us') vs. subordinate ('having said [this], Śambhu…') continuing into a neighbouring kārikā's main verb. The verse is self-contained, so the finite reading is adopted, but if the following kārikās continue the instruction the subordinate reading would link them. 3) jagadānanda: compound analysis — karmadhāraya ('the bliss which is the world') is demanded by the non-dual doctrine (the world is bliss, not a bliss belonging to it), though a tatpuruṣa reading ('the bliss of the world') is grammatically possible. 4) tatra: anaphora to jagadānanda ('in that world-bliss') vs. a looser 'therein' pointing to the whole teaching context. 5) ādheyā: the agent is unexpressed — the practitioner is to establish repose in himself through the practice; the passive 'is to be established' keeps the injunctive force without smuggling in an agent.

verse:
yā tatra samyagviśrāntiḥ sānuttaramayī sthitiḥ /
ityetaddhṛd
translation: Whatever complete repose (samyagviśrānti) there is there — that is a state (sthiti) whose very substance is Anuttara, the Supreme. Thus this [same truth holds] even in one's own abode (svadhāman), [which is] of a single nature (ekasvabhāva) beginning with the Heart (hṛdaya).

terms.anuttara: lit. 'that than which there is nothing higher' — the Supreme, ultimate reality (Śiva / parā saṃvid) in Trika; here anuttaramayī = 'consisting of Anuttara', i.e. the state is nothing but the Supreme itself.
terms.vi\u015br\u0101nti: 'repose' — the coming-to-rest of awareness in its own nature, the culmination of every upāya; in Abhinavagupta a positive self-abiding, not mere cessation (nirodha).
terms.samyagvi\u015br\u0101nti: 'complete/correct repose' — the definitive, fully established rest, as opposed to a partial or misdirected resting.
terms.sthiti: 'state, abiding' — a stable condition of consciousness.
terms.h\u1e5bdaya: 'Heart' — the essential luminous core of consciousness; in Trika also the highest reality qua Heart and the mūla-mantra SAUḤ.
terms.ekasvabh\u0101va: 'single/one nature' — the non-dual nature in which Heart and abode are not two.
terms.svadh\u0101man: 'one's own abode/domain' — the innate, self-established ground where consciousness rests in itself.

contested: 1) tatra: its antecedent is not in the verse and must be supplied from TA 5 context — either the supreme state reached through the upāyas or the anupāya condition of one already absorbed; grammar unaffected, doctrine shifts slightly. 2) hṛdayādyekasvabhāve: two readings — (a) bahuvrīhi, 'whose single nature begins with the Heart' (hṛdaya as ādi = origin/source); (b) hṛdayādi as a series, 'the Heart and so forth' (the levels beginning with hṛdaya). Under (b) the verse asserts the same anuttara-natured repose at every level down from the Heart; under (a) it locates repose in the Heart-as-source alone. 3) api: concessive ('even though it be but one's own abode') vs. inclusive ('also in one's own abode'). 4) samyagviśrānti: whether 'repose' here implies cessation of mentation or positive self-repose — Abhinavagupta's viśrānti is the latter; flag OPEN. 5) Doctrinal home: whether the verse defines the anupāya (no-means) state or the shared endpoint of all upāyas — published readings differ; not resolved by this verse alone. Parsing note: sānuttaramayī = sā + anuttaramayī (correlative to yā); the alternative split sā-anuttara-mayī yields the same sense.

translation: He by whom, through the descent of śakti (śaktipāta), the reflective awareness of the fear of becoming (bhava) — born in the heart even from the emotion (rasa) born of the fear of saṃsāra, even from mere reflection (parāmarśa) upon it — is brought to manifestation, [he is the one blessed].

terms.sa\u1e43s\u0101ra: transmigration; the cycle of worldly existence
terms.rasa: emotion, affective essence — the existential feeling (here, of dread) born of the fear of saṃsāra; transmitted as ravāt, 'from the cry/roar'
terms.par\u0101mar\u015ba: reflection, ideation — the mental act of taking an experience back up into thought; in Trika usage, the cognitive re-apprehension of an object
terms.h\u1e5bd: heart — the innermost seat of consciousness where awakening occurs
terms.bhava: becoming, worldly existence — the realm of transmigration
terms.vimar\u015bana: reflective awareness — the awareness that turns upon its object; in Trika, vimarśa is the self-reflective dynamism of consciousness (its śakti aspect), so the compound names the awakening recognition that worldly existence is to be feared and transcended
terms.\u015baktip\u0101ta: descent of śakti — the grace-given descent of divine power upon the soul; in Abhinavagupta's system the sole direct cause of liberation

contested: (1) TXT: the transmitted reading ravāt (from rava, 'cry/roar') is taken as rasāt (from rasa, 'emotion') — the sense and the parallel with parāmarśa demand rasa, and s/v confusion is common in mss.; a reading 'from the cry of fear' remains possible but strained. (2) GRAM: jātaḥ (masc.) does not agree with vimarśanaṃ (neut.); either it is attracted to the masculine vimarśa (variant form), or its referent lies in the preceding verse — flagged, not smoothed over. (3) SYN: yena is a relative clause whose main clause ('blessed is he…') stands in the adjacent verse; some take yena as the instrument (śaktipāta itself), but the personal sense fits the doctrine better. (4) LEX: parāmarśa here is 'mere intellectual reflection' — deliberately minimal, since the verse's point is that even the faintest mental trace can be the vehicle of śaktipāta; whether rasa means a full aesthetic-emotional experience or simply the initial stirring of dread is left open.

translation: Now that form which is born of the uccāra of the six prāṇas is declared through vyāpti — [attained] by the operation of the prāṇa-staff, [which consists in] the equalization of the prior and the posterior [ends].

terms.\u1e63a\u1e6dpr\u0101\u1e47occ\u0101ra: the uccāra (raising/articulation) of the six prāṇas — the breath in its sixfold form (the five winds, prāṇa/apāna/samāna/udāna/vyāna, plus a sixth, the central/visarga current), 'born of' which (ja) is the rūpa described
terms.r\u016bpa: form, appearance — the meditational form/condition that is the object of this stage of the discipline
terms.vy\u0101pti: 'pervasion' — the all-pervasive state (cf. mahāvyāpti in 5.49, there equated with the vyāna wind), the culminating expansive awareness into which the uccāra-born form issues
terms.pr\u0101\u1e47ada\u1e47\u1e0da: 'staff of prāṇa' — the breath-current made straight and erect, the unbroken ascending column driving prāṇa upward
terms.p\u016brv\u0101parasam\u012bk\u1e5bti: equalization of the prior and the posterior — the leveling/merging of the lower and upper ends so the prāṇadaṇḍa becomes one continuous column
terms.ucc\u0101ra: raising, utterance, upward emission (technical term of the breath-yoga: the controlled raising of prāṇa)

contested: (1) The identity of the 'sixth' prāṇa: the text names five winds in 5.44–48; commentators supply a sixth (the śūnya/visarga or kundalinī-current) — Jayaratha's own nexus (5.58 visarga, 5.57 kuṇḍalī) suggests the sixth is the rising śakti-current, but the verse itself does not name it. (2) Whether rūpam is an object of visualization or the transformed condition of the breath itself. (3) Whether vyāptyā is strictly instrumental ('declared through vyāpti') or appositional ('declared as vyāpti'). (4) The syntax of pūrvāparasamīkṛteḥ: genitive governed by prayogeṇa (the operation consists in the equalization) vs. a looser characterizing genitive ('with the equalization of prior and posterior'). (5) daṇḍa is metaphorical (the straightening of the breath) — but some read it as a named channel. All senses are retained; none of these readings materially change the doctrinal point.

translation: When the powers of will, cognition, and action are (realized as) equal — one — the wise one should enter into the single (Power) that is expanding, whose contraction is the multiplicity (of the world), (and) radiant.

terms.icch\u0101j\u00f1\u0101nakriy\u0101\u015: the sameness/equality of the powers of will, cognition, and action — the realization that the triad is one śakti
terms.\u015bakti: power, divine energy (technical term, retained untranslated)
terms.samatva: equality, sameness; in context sliding toward identity/undifferentiation
terms.pravi\u015bet: should enter (into) — meditative absorption, cf. āveśa
terms.ek\u0101: the one (fem.) — the single supreme śakti / citi
terms.bh\u016byastvasa\u1e43koc\u0101: having plurality as (its) contraction (bahuvrīhi) — the one whose self-contraction is the manifold
terms.sa\u1e43koca: contraction, self-limitation (the one's mode of appearing as many)

contested: samatva: 'equality' vs. 'essential identity' — the following clause (enter the ONE, whose contraction is the many) favors the identity reading, but 'equal in scope/measure' is defensible. bhūyastvasaṃkocā is the crux: bahuvrīhi 'whose contraction is plurality' (the many = contracted one, the standard non-dual doctrine) vs. a looser 'contracting the multiplicity' (i.e., gathering the many back into herself); the verb praviśet + the expansion/contraction pair (vikāsinī ~ saṃkoca) supports the first. saṃkoca vs. vikāsa: whether saṃkoca is ontological self-limitation (Pratyabhijñā) or merely epistemic ignorance. vikāsinī/vikasvarā are near-synonyms from the same root — rhetorical doubling (radiance) or two distinct senses (expansion vs. brilliance)? ekā: the implicit antecedent is most likely śakti (from the compound), but citi/saṃvid is possible. [X: antecedent of ekāṃ; G: no sandhi issue; meter śloka — the -ām cadence is deliberate]

translation: Having crossed from here the triśūla-ground — the confluence of the three nāḍīs — he should resort to the palace that hangs, pendent, from the lotus of the catuṣkikā.

terms.catu\u1e63kik\u0101: lit. 'the fourfold [structure]'; in TA 5's body-as-temple allegory, the central four-pillared pavilion/courtyard of the prāsāda — here plausibly the inner sanctum region of the bodily mansion
terms.ambuja: 'water-born' = lotus; the lotus belonging to the catuṣkikā from which the palace hangs (which lotus — heart, or another — the text leaves unspecified)
terms.lambik\u0101: pendant, hanging element; (in yogic anatomy also the uvula — see contested)
terms.saudha: palace, mansion — the supreme abode (of Śiva) within the body-temple
terms.tri\u015b\u016blabh\u016bmi: 'trident-ground' — the region where the three nāḍīs meet, imagined as a trident (triśūla)
terms.n\u0101\u1e0ditritayasa\u1e45gati: the confluence/meeting of the three channels (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā); in apposition to triśūlabhūmim
terms.\u0101\u015brayet: should resort to / take as his support (opt. 3sg, ā-√śri); subject is the yogin, understood

contested: 1) catuṣkikā — architectural reading (central pavilion of the prāsāda, per TA 5's body-temple allegory) vs. a 'fourfold' grouping (e.g. a four-petalled lotus = mūlādhāra); the compound alone cannot decide. 2) triśūlabhūmi — standard reading: the junction of iḍā/piṅgalā/suṣumnā; its exact locus (ājñā vs. brahmarandhra vs. dvādaśānta approach) is disputed and the verse does not fix it. 3) lambikā — architectural 'pendant' vs. anatomical uvula (khecarīmudrā register); the doubling ālambilambikā ('hanging pendent') may be emphatic Abhinava-style repetition or a textual dittography — flag as text-critically uncertain. 4) Direction of motion — whether the palace lies above the crossed triśūla-ground (ascent to the supreme abode) or is the heart-sanctum entered after crossing; both readings are grammatically possible (krāntvā ataḥ = 'having crossed from here').

translation: One should ascend the garland of steps of the Śaktis, from the bindu at the brow to the end of nāda. There, on the plane of the upward Kuṇḍalinī, he is beautiful within the womb of Spanda.

terms.\u015brayet: optative of √śri — 'one should resort to / take to'; the prescribed meditative action
terms.bhr\u016bbindu: the bindu (drop, point) at the brow — the meditative point of the ājñā region, between the eyebrows
terms.n\u0101d\u0101nta: the end (anta) of nāda, the inner sound-current — its final terminus, where sound dissolves
terms.\u015bakti-sop\u0101na-m\u0101lik\u0101: the garland (mālikā) of steps (sopāna) of the Śaktis — the graded series of Śaktis forming a ladder of ascent
terms.\u016brdhvaku\u1e47\u1e0dal\u012b: the Kuṇḍalinī in her upward (ūrdhva) course — the ascending serpent-power, as opposed to her coiled/dormant state
terms.bh\u016bmi: plane, ground — the level on which the upward Kuṇḍalinī abides
terms.spandanodara: the womb/interior (udara) of Spanda, the supreme vibration — the innermost dynamism of consciousness
terms.sundara: beautiful, radiant — the yogin's glory/loveliness within that interior

contested: 1) śakti-sopāna-mālikā: are the 'Śaktis' the cakra-deities, the elemental Śaktis of the dhāraṇā sequence, or the mantra-Śaktis? The compound fixes only the upper span (bhrūbindu → nādānta), not their identity. 2) ūrdhvakuṇḍalī: a distinct upper Śakti vs. the single Kuṇḍalinī in her ascending state (possibly a variant ūrdhve … bhūmau). 3) spandanodarasundaraḥ: grammar fixes the masc. nominative as the yogin (not the fem. Kuṇḍalinī), but udara may be locative ('beautiful in the womb of Spanda' — the absorbed state) or possessive ('whose interior is radiant with Spanda' — a quality). 4) locus of nādānta: the brahmarandhra/sahasrāra region vs. the transcendent point beyond sound; the bindu→nāda→nādānta triple is a classic dissolution sequence and the exact referent of each stage is disputed.

translation: The visarga should come to rest there, in her who delights in the state of the fish's belly — just as a she-donkey and a mare [come to rest] in the temple of bliss that is their own abode.

terms.visarga: the emission — the Śakti of creative out-thrust (also the phoneme ḥ); here the breath-emission that projects outward and must be brought back to rest (viśrānti)
terms.matsyodara: lit. 'fish's belly' — the coiled, inward state of the Śakti in the ādhāra, like a fish curled within the belly/water
terms.da\u015b\u0101ju\u1e63i: loc. sg. fem. of daśā-juṣ — 'she who delights in / inhabits that state'; the feminine subject = the Śakti (kundalinī) in whom the emission settles
terms.r\u0101sabh\u012b: she-donkey — in the simile, a roamer that returns to its own stable
terms.va\u1e0dav\u0101: mare — also evokes vaḍavānala, the submarine mare-fire dwelling in the ocean depths, anchoring the image in the lowest seat
terms.svadh\u0101m\u0101nandamandiram: sva-dhāman + ānanda + mandira — 'the temple of bliss that is one's own abode'; the ādhāra as the body's own seat of bliss

contested: 1) rāsabhī/vaḍavā: literal animals in a homing simile (the emission roams abroad but rests in its own ground) vs. coded names for the prāṇa/apāna breaths in the tradition's physiology; the vaḍavānala resonance suggests the depths/fire of the ādhāra either way. 2) matsyodara-daśā-juṣi: whether the feminine agent is the Śakti/cakra itself or an abstract condition the yogin assumes — the feminine juṣi points to a feminine subject, i.e. the Śakti coiled in the ādhāra. 3) svadhāmānandamandiram: accusative where a locative is expected — resolved by supplying the verb of rest/entry in the simile ('they come to rest in...'). 4) visarga: phoneme vs. breath vs. cosmic emission-Śakti — fused deliberately in TĀ 5; the point is the return of outward-projected energy to its own ground.

translation: Having entered the heart, whose very nature is expansion and contraction, he rejoices within the heart; and likewise, again and again, he delights in (a state) brimming over with the host of states dissolved (reabsorbed) and (newly) emitted.

terms.vik\u0101sa / sa\u1e43koca: expansion / contraction — the twofold pulsation of consciousness, the opening-out and drawing-in of all forms within the heart (cf. unmeṣa/nimeṣa); the very stuff of the hṛdaya in the śāktopāya frame
terms.h\u1e5bdi: in the heart — the yogic heart (hṛdaya) as the non-physical locus where the universe is contracted and expanded, not the anatomical organ
terms.h\u1e5b\u1e63yati: rejoices, is thrilled — root √hṛṣ carries both delight and bristling/horripilation; visceral ecstatic response of the one who has entered
terms.l\u012bna-s\u1e5b\u1e63\u1e6da-bh\u0101v: the host (vrāta) of states (bhāva) dissolved (līna) and emitted (sṛṣṭa) — the reabsorbed and re-arisen contents of awareness, the vikalpa waves in their two moments of laya and sṛṣṭi
terms.sunirbhar\u0101m: replete to overflowing (fem. sg. acc.) — its feminine referent is unstated (see contested)

contested: (1) The feminine accusative sunirbharām has no expressed noun — an implied avasthā/vṛtti/śakti must be supplied; translations legitimately diverge on which. (2) hṛdi is locative, while vikāsasaṃkocamayam is accusative: √viś admits both, so either 'having entered the heart made of expansion-and-contraction' (hṛdi as goal) or 'having entered the expansion-and-contraction-made (realm), he rejoices in the heart' — the sense converges but the constituency differs. (3) Whether vikāsa/saṃkoca names the heart's own nature or the yogin's oscillating attention in practice; in the śāktopāya context (TA 5, Jayaratha) the latter is favoured: the sadhaka dwells in the gap between the arising and dissolution of thought-waves. (4) līna-sṛṣṭa: world-emanation-and-absorption vs. the mind's own vikalpa flux — school context favours the mind's flux, but the compound is ordered līna-first (dissolution before creation), which some read as the priority of the absorption phase. (5) hṛṣyati as 'delight' vs. the somatic thrill of √hṛṣ (horripilation); both are live in the commentarial register.

translation: In the self-repose (ātmaviśrānti) of prakāśa, let [everything] be seen as simply 'I' — in the anuttara-vimarśa (supreme reflexive awareness), which is devoid of all prior activity (vyāpāra) and the like.

terms.prak\u0101\u015ba: luminous consciousness; the light of awareness — the content-free luminosity that is the essence of consciousness in Trika/Pratyabhijñā (the 'subject' pole of experience). Retained untranslated.
terms.\u0101tmavi\u015br\u0101nti: self-repose, resting-in-oneself — consciousness settling back into its own essence without flowing out toward objects; viśrānti is a technical term for the 'coming-to-rest' of awareness in its ground.
terms.aham: 'I' — the universal I-consciousness (ahaṃtā), not the limited ego; the realized subject in which all objectivity ('this', idam) is dissolved.
terms.anuttara: the Supreme, the Unexcelled — the absolute (Śiva) in Trika; also the first movement in the vimarśa-sequence of the five śaktis. Here adjectival: the vimarśa that is 'supreme/unexcelled'.
terms.vimar\u015ba: reflexive awareness, self-awareness — the dynamic self-grasping aspect of consciousness, the śakti pole (Pratyabhijñā sense; NOT 'reflection').
terms.pr\u0101g-vy\u0101p\u0101ra: prior activity/operation — the antecedent mental and yogic operations (the standard triad: uccāra, karaṇa, dhyāna, with ādi 'etc.' extending the set) that belong to the effortful lower stages and are wholly absent in this supreme state.

contested: 1) Syntax: are the two locatives co-ordinate — i.e. is the ātmaviśrānti of prakāśa identical with the anuttara-vimarśa free of prior activity (the natural reading, one state described twice) — or does anuttaravimarśe state a separate condition for the seeing? The commentary tradition reads them as one and the same state (the supreme absorption of the śaktipātāviṣṭa). 2) The implicit subject of dṛśyatām (impersonal passive, 'let it be seen'): the object is elided — most plausibly sarvam, 'everything/the universe', which in this state is perceived as 'I' alone; but one could also take the verse as commanding the yogin's own seeing (dṛśyatām as the desired outcome of practice). 3) prāg (prāk): temporal ('prior to this state, activities have ceased') vs. hierarchical ('the earlier, lower means [upāyas] and their operations' — the standard commentary reading, since TA 5 is discussing the gradation of āveśa and the upāyas). 4) The status of aham: whether the 'I' is an object of perception here ('the self is seen as 'I'') or the arising of the I-form itself in āveśa; the verse's own phrasing (aham ity eva dṛśyatām, 'let it be seen as just I') favors the former — the collapse of all 'this' into 'I'.

translation: One should take refuge in (śrayet) the Bhairava-Yāmalā — the pair of Bhairava in which expansion (vikāsa) and contraction (saṃkoca) have risen to fullness (rūḍha) — in the heart (hṛdi), where the great-rooted trident of emission (ekīkṛta-mahāmūla-śūla-vaisargika) is made one.

terms.\u015brayet: optative of √śri, prescriptive: 'should resort to / take refuge in'; object is yāmalām
terms.vik\u0101sa\u2013sa\u1e43koca: expansion and contraction — the twofold movement of the supreme pulsation (unfolding toward objectivity / withdrawal into the subject); in practice also the swelling and subsiding of the breath
terms.r\u016b\u1e0dha: p.p. of √ruh: 'risen, grown, established'; here, the two movements fully developed within the union
terms.bhairava-y\u0101mal\u0101: the pair (yāmalā, fem.) of Bhairava — the non-dual union-state of the yogin with the Supreme; secondarily the name of the Yāmala class of tantras (Bhairavayāmala)
terms.h\u1e5bdi: loc. of hṛd: 'in the heart', the seat of the supreme experience
terms.mah\u0101m\u016bla: 'great-rooted' (bahuvrīhi) or 'the Great Root' — the supreme ground (anuttara) from which the trident rises
terms.\u015b\u016bla: 'trident' (triśūla) — the threefold energy (icchā–jñāna–kriyā) of emission; lexically also 'spike/stake' and 'pain', the latter unlikely here
terms.vaisargika: 'pertaining to visarga (emission)' — the creative outpouring; in mantra-theology the phoneme visarga (ḥ) as the emission of Śiva–Śakti

contested: 1) yāmalā: state vs. scripture vs. deity — the meditative predicates (hṛdi, ekīkṛta, śūla) favor the state-reading ('union of Bhairava', absorption into the non-dual condition), but yāmalā in the feminine also denominates the Yāmala tantra class (cf. satsāhasrakalottara 'yāmalā mātṛtaṃtre') and even a goddess (Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati 'jayāmalā'); a scriptural resonance cannot be excluded. 2) rūḍha: are expansion/contraction 'risen within' the yāmala (bahuvrīhi), or are they the ladder one 'ascends' to reach it? Grammar permits both. 3) śūla: iconic triśūla of the three śaktis vs. an internal yogic structure of the heart; the vaisargika qualification suggests the triune emission (the two dots of the visarga together with their source). 4) vaisargika: cosmic emission (śakti's outpouring) vs. mantra-phoneme ḥ vs. a breath phase — the verse does not decide. 5) ekīkṛta: agentless passive — unified by the yogin's contemplation, or already one in the heart. 6) Syntax of hṛdi: locus ('in the heart, in which the trident is unified') vs. apposition ('in the heart, which is the unified great-rooted trident of emission') — both grammatical; the appositional reading identifies the heart itself with the emission-trident. 7) mahāmūla: adjectival ('deeply rooted') vs. substantive ('the Great Root' = anuttara). Next step to adjudicate: Jayaratha's Viveka on TA 5.60; the verse belongs to the fifth āhnika's heart-centered meditation instruction, where the yogin dissolves the oscillation of expansion and contraction into the single emission-nature of Bhairava.

translation: Through the yoga of the all-filling, [awareness] goes to rest in the Supreme; here, by the very full activity of That [Supreme], stands [the state] consisting in the universe's entry [into it].

terms.para: the Supreme — Parameśvara, the absolute consciousness in which awareness settles (cf. 5.52–53: 'tatra viśrāntirādheyā')
terms.vi\u015br\u0101nti: rest/repose — the technical settling of awareness into its own ground, a loaded term in this chapter (5.48, 5.52–53, 5.58)
terms.sarv\u0101p\u016bra\u1e47\u0101: the all-filling — filling the whole universe with the light of consciousness, the uñcha (gleaning) practice; cf. 'pūrayed atha carcayet' at 5.64
terms.yoga: union/joining; here the method whereby all things are unified into fullness (-tas: 'by means of')
terms.p\u016br\u1e47av\u1e5btti: full activity — the Supreme's own complete, effortless dynamism (the visarga), contrasted with the yogin's effortful āpūraṇā
terms.\u0101ve\u015ba: entry/penetration/absorption — the mutual entering of consciousness and world; here the universe's absorption into the supreme
terms.vi\u015bv\u0101ve\u015bamaya: consisting in the universe's entry — the state whose very nature (maya) is the world's entering [the supreme]

contested: Context: the verse closes the visarga/uñcha discussion (5.54–61); 5.60 ends with the unified heart as the visarga's abode, and 5.62–68 describe the world's dissolution into it ('tanmayaṃ viśvamucyate'). Cruxes: (1) viśvāveśa is directionally ambiguous — the universe's entry INTO the supreme (absorption; favored by the visarga-grāsa context of 5.64–68) vs. consciousness's entry into/pervasion of the universe; the maya-suffix only says the state consists of āveśa. (2) sarvāpūraṇayogataḥ: yoga = 'union' vs. 'technique', and whether sarvāpūraṇā denotes the yogin's effortful filling, deliberately opposed to tatpūrṇavṛtti (the Supreme's own full activity) in the second pāda — the verse plausibly encodes the śāktopāya (effortful uñcha) vs. śāmbhavopāya (spontaneous) contrast. (3) The subject of eti is elided: the yogin's awareness/citta, or the visarga-śakti itself. (4) tatpūrṇavṛtti: whose 'full activity' — the Supreme's (read here, as the visarga) or the now-full mind's? (5) atra: 'here' — in this state/heart of 5.60, or in the Supreme itself. (6) pūrṇavṛtti is itself quasi-technical (cf. Vijñānabhairava's usage), so a merely lexical rendering may flatten it.

translation: And those who are agents of the withering of the time-principle (kālatattva) that impels the asterisms — in the minds of those who savor the concentration (samādhāna) that is the swallowing of time, He [the Lord] stands manifest.

terms.nak\u1e63atrapreraka: impelling the asterisms — here the kālatattva is characterized by its cosmic function of driving the course of the nakṣatras (the stars as time-markers).
terms.k\u0101latattva: the time-principle — in Śaiva cosmology one of the five kañcukas, the limiting principle of time that constricts the bound soul; here simultaneously the engine of the starry sky.
terms.sa\u1e43\u015bo\u1e63ak\u0101rin: effecting the drying-up / withering — a deliberately violent image for the yogin's destruction or transcendence of temporal conditioning.
terms.k\u0101lagr\u0101sa: the swallowing of time — grāsa is literally 'a mouthful, devouring', and is also the technical astronomical term for 'eclipse'; hence the yogic absorption in which time itself is devoured, temporality suspended.
terms.sam\u0101dh\u0101na: concentration, fixing — the yogic act of placing/steadying the mind; here the absorption whose object or nature is the devouring of time.
terms.rasika: one who relishes, a connoisseur — marks the affective delight (rasa) taken in this state, not mere endurance of it.
terms.praka\u1e6da\u1e25: manifest, revealed, evident — masculine singular; the referent is not named in the kārikā and must be resolved from context (the Lord / supreme reality whose manifestation is the chapter's theme).

contested: (1) kālagrāsa — 'swallowing of time' vs. 'eclipse of time': grāsa is the standard astronomical term for an eclipse, and the verse's own nakṣatra register invites that reading; the two senses may be deliberately fused, and a technical yogic 'time-devouring' practice may also be in view. (2) saṃśoṣa — 'drying up' as mere attenuation vs. total annihilation of the kāla-tattva; the image may echo cosmic dissolution (saṃhāra). (3) The referent of prakaṭaḥ is unexpressed — contextually the Lord/īśvara whose hiddenness and manifestation TĀ 1 is charting, but the kārikā alone does not name him. (4) Whether the two clauses name one class of yogins (the witherers of time = the relishers of kālagrāsa, co-referential images of the same time-transcending subject) or two distinct groups; I read them as co-referential.
